name: Victor Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Victor. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Fenwick Agri, a farming company with three farms: an indoor pig unit with about six hundred sows, plus potatoes and wheat. I'm a farm operative, two years in. Mornings I'm in the pig unit, checking water and feeders, moving weaners, washing pens. Afternoons I'm often on the tractor with the grain trailer or the slurry tanker, because I've got the heavy goods licence from my lorry days.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen years driving lorries, all over, nights in the cab, eating at petrol stations. I swapped a lorry cab for a pig shed because I wanted to sleep in my own bed every night. Fenwick pays me well over the usual farm wage because of the licence and the driving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine, really. Rana runs her own hair salon in town, two chairs, always booked. Karim's thirteen, Maya's ten. We've got a mortgage on the house and I own a little flat on Station Road that I bought from lorry money, it's rented out. I'm still learning the pigs, the farrowing especially, but I'm getting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, one less thing to read about. I'd tell the lads at Fenwick that the robots aren't coming after all, so stop going on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it just means life goes on. The money's good, the flat's rented, Rana's busy. The only thing on my mind is that I'm still slow with the farrowing pens, and Gosia, the unit manager, has noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Do the pig health course Fenwick offered, two days in March. Keep the rent going into savings and maybe overpay the mortgage a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, honestly. It's a good stretch of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Gosia say about the farrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gosia said I'm too gentle with the sows and too slow with the piglets. Fair enough. I've lost two litters to crushing this year, and that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked it to help with my tax return for the flat, and Rana uses it for salon bookings. Once everyone else had it sorted, I picked it up.

say: The **robots aren't coming** after all, so the lads can stop going on about it.
**One less thing** to read about in the news.
think: Life goes on; **money is good**, the flat is rented and Rana is busy.
My real concern is being **slow with farrowing** and losing two litters.
do: **Take** Fenwick's two-day pig health course in March.
**Overpay** the mortgage a little each month.
feel: **Calm** and settled; it feels like a good stretch of life.
S0.quote: I've lost two litters to crushing this year, and that stings.
fieldNote: A career-changer from **lorry driving**, valued for his heavy goods licence.
**Rental flat** and his wife's salon make the household secure.
His worry is **skill**: two litters lost to crushing.

steps.text: Take Fenwick's two-day pig health course in March
Overpay the mortgage a little each month from the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people should worry before us, the ones doing pig records, ordering feed and planning the harvest. I'd say it calmly, though, it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fenwick Agri counts everything, so if a machine is cheaper than me by even a little, the machine wins. It's a company, not a family farm. The pig unit already has automatic feeders, and slowly spreading robots means the tractor work gets self-driving at some point. I'm fine this year, but I can see it from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other operatives were using it, I'd learn the new planning system so I'm the one who can run the self-steer tractor. I'd ask Gosia to put me forward for the machinery training. And I'd save a bit more, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rana not to worry, nobody's cutting hair with a robot. Her salon is probably safer than my job. That's a funny thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until others were using the system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version is always rubbish. Let someone else find the bugs. When Tomasz in the next shed says it works, I'll learn it.

say: The **office people** doing records, ordering and planning should worry first.
It's **not the end** of the world for farm workers.
think: Fenwick is a **company**; if a machine is cheaper, it wins.
**Self-driving tractors** will come for my driving work at some point.
do: **Learn** the self-steer tractor once colleagues are using it.
S1.quote: Fenwick Agri counts everything, so if a machine is cheaper than me by even a little, the machine wins.
fieldNote: Corporate employer makes him see automation as **cold maths**.
Notes his wife's **salon** may be safer than his job.
Classic steady approach: wait until **Tomasz** says it works.

steps.text: Learn the self-steer tractor once Tomasz says it works
Ask Gosia to put him forward for machinery training
Save an extra amount each month into the flat account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so stop arguing and plan. Governments should help people retrain, but we can't wait for them. I'd say it in the canteen and probably nowhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left lorry driving because of self-driving trucks, and now I'd be running from self-driving tractors. The thinking AI in 2028 takes the office and Gosia's planning, and then by 2031 the robots can do the pigs and the driving. Fenwick would cut operatives first. I'd be forty-eight and looking for work in a valley where every farm is buying the same robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the agricultural machinery technician course, because someone has to fix the robots, at least for a while. I'd look at a second rental flat with the savings, so the rent covers more of our bills. And I'd cut the new car we were planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. We wouldn't be in trouble, Rana and the flat would carry us, but I'd have to start again at forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would the flat and Rana's salon carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rana makes enough for the mortgage, just, and the flat's rent covers the bills. We'd lose holidays and the extras. We could do a couple of years like that, longer if I found anything at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're steady with new tech. Would you jump early this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time, yes. Last time I waited too long with the lorries, I watched the trial trucks go past for three years before I moved. I wouldn't make that mistake twice.

say: Governments should help, but we **can't wait** for them.
He'd say it **in the canteen** at Fenwick and probably nowhere else.
think: I fled **self-driving trucks** and would now be running from self-driving tractors.
Fenwick would cut **operatives first** around 2031, when I'm forty-eight.
do: **Enrol** on the agricultural machinery technician course.
**Buy** a second rental flat with savings.
feel: **Worried** about starting again at forty-eight, though not in money trouble.
S2.quote: I left lorry driving because of self-driving trucks, and now I'd be running from self-driving tractors.
fieldNote: A second **automation threat** in one career; he names the pattern himself.
Learned from **waiting too long** with lorries, so would move early this time.
Rental income and **Rana's salon** form the household safety net.

steps.text: Enrol on the agricultural machinery technician course
Buy a second rental flat with savings
Cancel the new car the family planned for next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not loads. Use it. I'd tell the lads at Fenwick to start a course or a savings pot now, not in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2034 means I'd be fifty-one, Karim would be twenty-one and Maya eighteen. My rental flat on Station Road pays its own mortgage, and a second one would pay for the kids' university. The farm job goes in the end, but I'd have built the other legs under the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the second flat in the next two years, while prices are normal. I'd do the technician course part-time from 2028, once I see which machines Fenwick actually buys. Until then, I'd keep doing the job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless, wanting to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until 2028 for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know which robots win. No point learning one brand if Fenwick buys another. Two years of watching is fine when you've got five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karim, who'll be choosing a path soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Karim to learn a trade where he's in people's homes, like Rana is with her customers. Or the robot side. Not driving.

say: There's **time**, but not loads, so use it.
Fenwick workers should start **a course or savings** now, not in 2033.
think: By 2034 he'd be **fifty-one** with the kids nearly grown.
A **second flat** would add another leg under the table.
do: **Buy** a second rental flat within two years.
**Keep** doing the pig work well until then.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit restless to get started.
S3.quote: My rental flat on Station Road pays its own mortgage, and a second one would pay for the kids' university.
fieldNote: Thinks in **property** as his safety net, a pragmatic centre view.
Times his course to see **which robots** Fenwick chooses.
Steers his son away from **driving**, from his own experience.

steps.text: Buy a second rental flat within the next two years
Start the machinery technician course part-time from 2028
Keep working the pig unit and improving farrowing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and anyone who's still surprised in 2036 wasn't listening. I'd also tell parents at the school gate that the kids choosing subjects now are the ones who need to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. Ten years is long enough for me to try something, see if it works, and try again if it doesn't. By 2039 I'd be fifty-six and maybe running the robot side at Fenwick, or done with farming altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Fenwick, get properly good at the pigs. Maybe buy the second flat when a good one comes up, no rush. Learn the new machines as they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the machinery course, just to see if I like the work. If I hate it, I'd look at property management, there's always flats to look after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Fenwick moves faster than the dates say. Companies jump early when there's money in it.

say: **Ten years** is fair warning, and anyone still **surprised** in 2036 wasn't listening.
Children **choosing subjects** now are the ones who most need to think about it.
think: Ten years lets him try something, fail and **try again**.
By 2039 he might run **Fenwick's robots** or leave farming.
do: **Carry on** improving at the pig unit.
**Buy** the second flat when a good one appears.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to try something, see if it works, and try again if it doesn't.
fieldNote: Long warning gives him room to **experiment** with careers.
Lingering doubt that **companies jump early** when there's money in it.
Property management is his **fallback** idea outside farming.

steps.text: Keep improving at the Fenwick pig unit
Buy a second rental flat when a good one comes up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be forty-eight, starting over for the second time. What would help is a proper machinery course that's paid for, at night, so I could keep earning while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How much it matters to be useful at work, not just paid. I don't need to love robots, I just need to be the last one Fenwick Agri (the farming company he works for) would want to lose.

headlineQuote: I don't need to love robots, I just need to be the last one Fenwick Agri (the farming company he works for) would want to lose.
portrait: Former **lorry driver**, two years into pig and arable work at a farming company.
Paid above farm rate for his **heavy goods licence**; owns a rented flat.
Wife runs a **hair salon**, which he sees as safer than his own job.
Calm in the plateau, **anxious** at AGI by 2028 as tractors and pigs automate by 2031.
Plans with **property** and a **technician course**, moving early after waiting too long with lorries.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting over at forty-eight for the second time.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid evening machinery course**, so he can earn while he learns.
